title: RIGHT JOIN
objective: Read and write RIGHT JOIN as a mirrored LEFT JOIN: keep every row of the table written SECOND, and be able to rewrite any RIGHT JOIN as a LEFT JOIN by swapping table order.
context: You will meet RIGHT JOINs in inherited queries and generated SQL. Most teams standardise on LEFT JOIN, but you must read RIGHT JOIN fluently — and know which table it protects.

exercises.title: Every supplier and its products (RIGHT JOIN)
exercises.question: Procurement wants every supplier with each of its products, including suppliers with none.
exercises.prompt: Write FROM products ... RIGHT JOIN suppliers. Return supplier_id (from suppliers), supplier_name and product_name — one row per supplier–product pair, plus one row with NULL product_name for any supplier without products.
hints: products is written first → it's the left table; suppliers is the right table and must all survive.
Take supplier_id from s, not p — p.supplier_id is NULL for the unmatched supplier.
SELECT s.supplier_id, s.supplier_name, p.product_name FROM products p RIGHT JOIN suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id;
exercises.why: Knowing which side a RIGHT JOIN protects lets you read legacy SQL correctly.

recall.q: In `FROM a RIGHT JOIN b`, which table keeps all its rows?

exercises.join_notes: products 25, suppliers 5. Result: 24 rows = 23 matched product rows (suppliers repeat: 6, 6, 6 and 5 times — one-to-many) + 1 row for supplier 5 'Andes Trading' with product_name NULL. Products 21 (supplier 9) and 22 (NULL supplier) are dropped: they are on the LEFT side, which a RIGHT JOIN does not protect.

exercises.title: All orders with customer names, orphan included
exercises.question: Finance wants every order with its customer name — no order may go missing.
exercises.prompt: Write FROM customers ... RIGHT JOIN orders. Return order_id, order_date and customer_name (customers.name; NULL when the customer does not exist) for all 60 orders.
hints: Which table must survive completely? It is written second, so use RIGHT JOIN.
This equals FROM orders LEFT JOIN customers.
FROM customers c RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
exercises.why: Revenue reconciliation demands every fact row survive the dimension lookup — orphans must be visible, not lost.

recall.q: Rewrite `FROM customers c RIGHT JOIN orders o ON ...` as a LEFT JOIN.
recall.a: FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON ... (swap the tables).

exercises.join_notes: customers 20, orders 60. Result: 60 rows — every order survives and each matches at most one customer, so no multiplication. Order 31 (customer_id 99) gets customer_name NULL. Customers 18, 19, 20 (no orders) do not appear: they are in the left table, which RIGHT JOIN does not protect. An INNER JOIN would give 59 rows.

exercises.title: Units sold per product, zero included
exercises.question: Inventory wants units sold for EVERY product in the catalogue (all statuses), 0 for never-sold items.
exercises.prompt: Write FROM order_items ... RIGHT JOIN products. Return product_id (from products), product_name and units_sold (SUM of quantity; 0 when never sold) for all 25 products.
hints: products is the protected table → it goes second with RIGHT JOIN.
Group by the products columns (p.product_id), and COALESCE the SUM.
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, COALESCE(SUM(oi.quantity), 0) AS units_sold FROM order_items oi RIGHT JOIN products p ON ... GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
exercises.why: Grouping by the protected table's key is essential: grouping by oi.product_id would merge all unmatched products into one NULL group.

recall.q: Why GROUP BY p.product_id and not oi.product_id here?
recall.a: oi.product_id is NULL for never-sold products; grouping by it would collapse them into one NULL row.

exercises.join_notes: order_items 150, products 25. Before grouping: 153 rows = 150 matched lines (products repeat once per line — product 9 fifteen times) + 3 NULL-padded rows for never-sold products 23, 24, 25. After GROUP BY: 25 rows; those three show units_sold 0 thanks to COALESCE (SUM of NULLs is NULL).

exercises.title: Customers who never ordered (RIGHT anti-join)
exercises.question: Marketing wants the sign-ups who have never placed any order.
exercises.prompt: Write FROM orders ... RIGHT JOIN customers. Return customer_id, name and signup_date of customers with no orders at all.
hints: Mirror of the LEFT anti-join: now the NULL-padded side is the LEFT table (orders).
Test the left table's primary key for NULL.
FROM orders o RIGHT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
exercises.why: Never-converted sign-ups are the cheapest audience to re-engage — you already have their details.

recall.q: In a RIGHT anti-join, which table's key do you test for NULL?
recall.a: The LEFT table's (the one written first, which gets NULL-padded).

exercises.join_notes: orders 60, customers 20. The RIGHT JOIN produces 62 rows: 59 order rows matched to customers (one-to-many) + 3 NULL-padded rows for customers 18 'Mia Lewis', 19 'alice johnson' and 20 'Zoe Turner'. Order 31 (customer 99) is dropped because it is on the unprotected left side. WHERE o.order_id IS NULL keeps the 3 never-ordered customers.

exercises.title: Electronics products per supplier — filter on the left side
exercises.question: Category management wants, for EVERY supplier, how many Electronics products they supply (0 if none).
exercises.prompt: Write FROM products ... RIGHT JOIN suppliers. Return supplier_id, supplier_name and electronics_count (number of products with category = 'Electronics'; 0 when none) for all 5 suppliers.
hints: The category filter is on products — the NULL-padded (left) side of this RIGHT JOIN.
In WHERE it would remove suppliers with no Electronics; put it in ON.
RIGHT JOIN suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id AND p.category = 'Electronics' ... COUNT(p.product_id)
exercises.why: Same trap as LEFT JOIN, mirrored: a WHERE on the unprotected table quietly turns an outer join into an inner join.

recall.q: In `a RIGHT JOIN b`, where does a filter on table a belong if all rows of b must survive?

exercises.join_notes: Only products with category 'Electronics' are allowed to match. Before grouping: 9 rows = 6 matched Electronics products (supplier 1: 2, supplier 4: 4 — product 22 is Electronics but has no supplier) + 3 NULL-padded rows for suppliers 2, 3 and 5. Result: 5 rows, three with electronics_count 0. Moving p.category = 'Electronics' to WHERE would return only 2 rows (suppliers 1 and 4).

exercises.title: Lines sold vs. lines returned per product
exercises.question: Quality wants, per sold product, how many order lines were sold, how many were returned and the total refunded.
exercises.prompt: Write FROM returns ... RIGHT JOIN order_items. Return product_id, lines_sold (number of order lines, any status), lines_returned (number of those lines with a return) and total_refunded (SUM of refund_amount rounded to 2 decimals; 0 when none), one row per product that appears in order_items.
hints: Every order line must survive; returns is optional → returns first, order_items second, RIGHT JOIN.
COUNT(r.return_id) counts only lines that matched a return.
FROM returns r RIGHT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_item_id = r.order_item_id GROUP BY oi.product_id
exercises.why: Return rates need both numerator and denominator in one pass; an INNER JOIN would leave only returned lines and a 100% return rate.

recall.q: What would an INNER JOIN between returns and order_items do to lines_sold?
recall.a: It would only keep the 10 returned lines, so lines_sold would equal lines_returned.

exercises.join_notes: returns 10, order_items 150. The RIGHT JOIN keeps all 150 lines: 10 match a return, 140 are NULL-padded on the returns side. No multiplication, because each line has at most one return. Grouped: 22 rows (the 22 products ever sold; 23–25 never appear in order_items). lines_returned totals 10 and total_refunded totals 690.80; most products show 0 returned and 0.00 refunded — those zeros come from NULL-padded rows.

worked_example.question: List every supplier with each of its products, written with RIGHT JOIN.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT s.supplier_id,
       s.supplier_name,
       p.product_name
FROM products AS p
RIGHT JOIN suppliers AS s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id
ORDER BY s.supplier_id DESC, p.product_name
LIMIT 5;
worked_example.explanation: suppliers is written second, so it is the right table and every supplier survives. Andes Trading (supplier 5) has no products: its product_name is NULL. Swap the tables and use LEFT JOIN for the same result.

recipe:
**The join recipe — do it in this order, every time, before typing SQL**

1. **Pick the driving table.** Which table's rows is the answer *about*? ("every customer…", "each order line…")
   That table goes first, after `FROM` — it is the **left table**.
2. **Name the right table(s) and the shared key.** What column links them? Is it PK → FK (one-to-many) or
   one-to-one? Which side is the "many" side?
3. **Ask: "must every row of the left table survive, even with no match?"**
   - no → `INNER JOIN` (unmatched rows silently disappear)
   - yes → `LEFT JOIN` (unmatched rows stay, right-side columns become NULL)
   - rows from *both* sides must survive → `FULL OUTER JOIN`
4. **Predict the row count before you run it.** Count the inputs (`SELECT COUNT(*) …`), think about
   matches per row (0, 1 or many), write your guess down — then run and compare. A surprise means
   you misunderstood the grain, the key or the data.

**RIGHT JOIN = LEFT JOIN with the tables written the other way round.**
The **left table is always the one written first** (after FROM); the right table is the one after JOIN.
RIGHT JOIN keeps **every row of the right table** and NULL-pads the left table's columns.

```sql
-- these two return the same rows:
SELECT s.supplier_name, p.product_name
FROM   products AS p                -- left table (written first)
RIGHT JOIN suppliers AS s           -- right table: every supplier survives
        ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id;

SELECT s.supplier_name, p.product_name
FROM   suppliers AS s
LEFT JOIN products AS p ON p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id;
```

For RIGHT JOIN, ask the recipe question about the **right** table: "must every row of the right table survive?"
- Filters on the protected (right) table → WHERE. Filters on the left (NULL-padded) table → ON.
- Anti-join: `FROM a RIGHT JOIN b ON … WHERE a.key IS NULL` → rows of b with no match in a.
- Style tip: in your own code prefer LEFT JOIN with the driving table first; read RIGHT JOIN by mentally swapping.
common_mistakes: Thinking 'left table' means the table on the left of the = sign. It is the table written first in FROM.
Grouping or selecting the key from the NULL-padded side (p.supplier_id instead of s.supplier_id).
Filtering the NULL-padded (left) table in WHERE, turning the RIGHT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
Mixing LEFT and RIGHT JOINs in one query — hard to reason about; rewrite as all LEFT JOINs.
recall: Which table does `FROM a RIGHT JOIN b` protect?
Rewrite `FROM a RIGHT JOIN b ON …` as a LEFT JOIN.
FROM b LEFT JOIN a ON …
In a RIGHT JOIN, which table's columns become NULL for unmatched rows?
review_next: Lesson 13 combines both directions: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides — perfect for reconciliations like 'customers without orders AND orders without customers'.
